tasks.q: When is a MAC address given to a device?
a: When its network interface card is made
Every time it joins a network
tasks.fb: The manufacturer sets it, and it is meant to stay the same.
MAC addresses are six pairs of hexadecimal digits.

tasks.q: What is an IP address used for?
a: Identifying a device so packets can be routed to it across networks
tasks.fb: Routers read the destination IP address to decide where to send each packet next.

tasks.q: Which device mainly uses IP addresses to forward data?
tasks.fb: Switches use MAC addresses inside a LAN; routers use IP addresses between networks.

tasks.q: Which is a valid IPv4 address?
How many bits are in an IPv4 address?
tasks.fb: Four numbers of 8 bits each makes 32 bits.

a: The world was running out of IPv4 addresses
tasks.fb: Billions of phones, computers and smart devices need addresses.

tasks.q: How many bits are in an IPv6 address?
tasks.fb: 128 bits gives an enormous number of possible addresses.

tasks.q: Which address does a switch use to deliver a frame?
tasks.fb: Switches work within a LAN, using MAC addresses.

tasks.q: Which address stays with a device when it moves to a different network?
tasks.fb: The MAC is built into the NIC; the IP address comes from the network it joins.

tasks.q: In the address 192.168.1.20, which part identifies the device?
tasks.fb: In this common home setup, the last number identifies the device.

tasks.q: Which address is on the same network as 192.168.1.20?
tasks.fb: It shares the same network part: 192.168.1.

tasks.q: Does each item describe a MAC, IPv4 or IPv6 address?
items: 48 bits, set when the NIC is made
Eight groups of hexadecimal separated by colons
Used by switches within a LAN

info.title: Hexadecimal
info.text: Hexadecimal uses 16 digits: 0 to 9, then A to F. Each pair of hex digits is exactly one byte, which is why MAC addresses are written in pairs.

info.title: Hiding your MAC
info.text: Many phones now use a random MAC address on each Wi-Fi network, so shops and venues can't track you from place to place.

info.title: Why 255?
info.text: Each part of an IPv4 address is 8 bits. The biggest number 8 bits can hold is 11111111 in binary, which is 255.

info.title: IPv4 ran out
info.text: The last big blocks of IPv4 addresses were handed out in 2011. Many networks now share one public address between many devices.

info.title: Home networks
info.text: Addresses starting 192.168 are private: they only work inside your home network. Your router shares one public IP address between all your devices.

info.title: Shortening IPv6
info.text: Groups of zeros in IPv6 can be shortened with ::, so 2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001 can be written as 2001:DB8::1.
